data.title: Texas Republican: 'I don't have an ounce of sympathy for Lindsay Clancy'
data.description:
Rep. Brandon Gill (R-Texas) said he has no sympathy for Lindsay Clancy after her murder trial ended in a mistrial, rejecting the defense’s argument that severe mental illness left her not criminally responsible for killing her three children.

“I don’t have an ounce of sympathy for Lindsay Clancy,” Gill said Friday on Fox News’s “The Will Cain Show.”

“I have an enormous amount of sympathy for the three little innocent kids who were slaughtered,” he said earlier.

Gill went on to push back against the central argument of Clancy’s defense: that she was experiencing postpartum psychosis when she strangled her three children — Cora, 5, Dawson, 3, and Callan, 8 months — at the family’s Massachusetts home in 2023.

“You don’t get licensed to murder your children or anybody else just because you have mental health problems,” Gill said. “We’ve gotten in a habit of medicalizing evil.”

Trial Judge William Sullivan declared a mistrial when jurors remained deadlocked for seven days without being able to reach a unanimous verdict on whether Clancy was criminally responsible for the killings.

A last-minute attempt was made by Clancy’s attorneys to remove the lone holdout juror, whom they accused of refusing to properly apply the legal standard of reasonable doubt. Sullivan declined to remove the juror.

The legal battle has dominated national headlines, with even President Trump weighing in to respond to news of the mistrial.

“It’s a shame. It’s a horrible tragedy,” Trump said when asked about the case during an executive order signing ceremony in the Oval Office. “She did a horrible, horrible thing.”

“I guess they’re going to go through another trial. It’s too bad,” he concluded.

data.title: Huckabee calls Israeli settler violence in West Bank an 'act of terror'
data.description:
U.S. Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee on Wednesday called Israeli settler violence in the West Bank an “act of terror,” condemning their actions.

Huckabee said his visit was for the U.S. citizens “who live in Turmusayya and other communities across this region” who are “disturbed by people who have created extraordinary challenges that are unfair and illegal.”

While acknowledging that he’s been “criticized a little bit for calling that terror,” he defended his statements as fitting the definition of terrorism in remarks at Turmusayya Town Hall, labeling these settlers as a “band of terrorists” engaged in “criminal activity.”

“It’s important that we continue to put the pressure to say letting a few people do these horrible activities of criminal nature is detrimental…to everyone, Israeli, Palestinian alike,” he said.

This isn’t the first time Huckabee has violent Israeli settlers as “terrorists.” In August, he condemned settlers for besieging a Palestinian village and the home of a Palestinian American in the West Bank town of Qusra. 

Huckabee said that the settlers burned a mosque and graffitied, “Huckabee, this is from the terrorist” on a wall in the village.

Huckabee’s continued remarks are an unusually strong response from the Trump administration related to Israeli settlers as President Trump previously dropped sanctions against violent Israeli settlers imposed by the Biden administration.

“I’m glad they admitted it,” Huckabee said Saturday about the message’s labeling. “I don’t think that’s what they intended to do, but I do think that they represent a very tiny minority.”

The State Department similarly condemned the violence, with a spokesperson saying last week that the department remains in line with the Trump administration’s goal to achieve peace in the region.

data.title: Former Stars and Stripes publisher: Pentagon lawsuit will 'continue on' after court setback
data.description:
Max Lederer, the former longtime publisher of the Stars and Stripes, on Saturday said he and the two other staffers fired by the Pentagon last month will “continue on” in their lawsuit after a federal judge denied their emergency request this week. 

Lederer and the paper’s former editor-in-chief, Erik Slavin, and reporter Lara Korte sued the Pentagon last week, alleging the department’s decision to dismiss them from their roles violated its own personnel rules and their First Amendment rights. 

U.S. District Judge Trevor McFadden ruled Friday that the employees were not likely to succeed in their claim that these terminations violated their First Amendment rights. 

Lederer told MS NOW’s Jacob Soboroff on Saturday morning that this request was only the “first step in the process,” noting that “it’s a really high bar in a preliminary injunction” and that McFadden’s ruling  “doesn’t eliminate our basic suit.”

“We are going on with that suit,” he said. “That will continue on, and we’ll have more opportunity to present our case to the judge and argue this very important issue.”

The Pentagon’s leadership under President Trump’s second presidency has attempted to reshape the military outlet’s coverage. Chief Pentagon Spokesperson Sean Parnell said in January that the department would “refocus” the organization’s coverage from “woke distractions that syphon morale.”

While the paper is staffed by members of the Defense Department, the Stars and Stripes has historically enjoyed editorial independence from the Pentagon. 

In March, the Pentagon issued an eight-page memo that included a requirement for the paper’s content to be “consistent with good order and discipline of the military.”

Two of the organization’s advisory board members sued the department in June, alleging the Pentagon was attempting to “exert unprecedented control” over the paper and sensor its content.

The department also removed the outlet’s ombudsman, Jacqueline Smith, whose job was to monitor the newspaper’s editorial independence. Smith sued the Pentagon in June over this decision.

Prior to his firing, Lederer had announced his retirement and planned to step down from his role overseeing the paper at the end of this month. He told MS NOW on Saturday that he made this decision after declining Pentagon officials’ request to fire two outlet staffers. 

“I had gotten to a point where I couldn’t support the direction any longer, and as any good employee of any good organization, your option is to do what you’re asked to do or leave,” Lederer said. “And I chose to leave.”

data.title: Bettors are harassing college athletes. It's time for Congress to act.
data.description:
Growing up, mom always said, “if you don’t have anything nice to say, then don’t say anything at all.” While she was unaware at the time, this phrase may become pointed legal advice — especially if you are a college sports fan or bettor.

College athletes across the country deal with abusive and vulgar messages from sports fans daily. Take Florida State forward Cam Corhen for example, who after being injured early in a basketball game and only scoring two points, returned to his phone filled with hateful messages from bettors, including one that said, “I hope your mom dies.” Or, North Carolina forward Armando Bacot, who received over one hundred messages demeaning him for having too few rebounds, just 12 days after North Carolina legalized player prop bets on collegiate sports.

Collegiate athlete harassment stemming from sports betting is a widespread issue. One in three high-profile athletes receive abusive messages from people with a betting interest. Student-athletes are demanded to strenuously prepare for their competitions multiple times per day, compete at a high level each week, and simultaneously, perform well academically. Beyond that, in the age of NIL, they are incentivized for maintaining extremely public-facing profiles online. These athletes face an impossible choice: build the public profile NIL demands or protect themselves from relentless online abuse.

Because these young athletes should not have to make such a decision at this stage in their lives, federal legislation is necessary to combat the issue. As legalized sports betting intensifies fan motivation to abusively target athletes, Congress must intervene by implementing a national banned bettors registry for individuals convicted of sports-related harassment and by allowing athletes to sue people who engage in repeated betting related harassment.

Now, it is easier than ever to place bets on individual players via prop bets that allow bettors to place wagers on specific player statistics. This gives fans greater cause to direct their harassment toward individual athletes. Some advocates even argue in favor of banning prop bets on college athletics or eliminating college sports betting altogether. However, because those courses of action are guaranteed to be met with fierce opposition advocacy by the gambling lobby and will take much longer to implement, federal legislation is a better, more expedient option.

This issue has not gone unnoticed, but the measures in place to deter or cure online abuse are failing. Social media or culture campaigns like the NCAA’s “Don’t Be a Loser” initiative encourage fans to be mindful of the statistics underlying gambling related harassment of student-athletes, but awareness campaigns lack teeth.

Additionally, the current legal framework underlying this issue is highly decentralized. Some states ban prop bets and others do not. Some implement banned bettor lists, and some prohibit all sports betting. This structure makes it impossible to protect all collegiate athletes across state lines.

To address this gap, Congress should implement a federal standard that targets online harassment tied to sports betting. First, federal legislation should impose criminal penalties for individuals who engage in online conduct that causes substantial emotional distress or fear for safety. A model for this approach can be found in a New York’s Senate Bill under consideration, which defines harassment in a way that captures the type of abusive and threatening messages these athletes routinely receive. The bill goes even further and designates those individuals convicted of harassment and stalking an amateur athlete as a prohibited sports bettor. A federal standard would ensure consistent treatment across jurisdictions.

Additionally, the legislation should allow collegiate athletes to sue individuals who engage in this type of abusive conduct. The ability to recover monetary damages would create a meaningful deterrent. Because much of this behavior is driven by financial frustration tied to lost wagers, attaching a financial penalty to that behavior directly targets the source of the problem.

Critics may attempt to mount free speech objections, but this narrowly tailored proposed solution is not aimed at criticism or negative commentary about athletic performance. The legislation would focus on true threats and targeted, repeated harassment toward a student-athlete. The Supreme Court has long recognized that speech made with the intent to threaten or intimidate is not protected under the First Amendment. Essentially, fans should feel free to criticize athletes, but not to terrorize them.

A federal approach would standardize accountability in ways state-by-state systems cannot. Rather than relying on inconsistent banned bettor lists and varying state regulations, national legislation would create a baseline level of protection for collegiate athletes, regardless of where they compete or where the harassment originates.

College athletes accept pressure when they step onto the field. They should not have to accept abuse when they step off it. Moving forward requires more than awareness; it requires accountability. Most importantly, it requires a commitment to protecting the well-being of the athletes who make college sports possible.

Deymon X. Fleming, Jr. is a J.D. candidate at the University of Georgia School of Law.

data.title: Kennedy Center closes after ceiling piece falls: 'President Trump has been right'
data.description:
A portion of the ceiling inside the Kennedy Center’s Grand Foyer collapsed Friday evening as heavy rain swept through the Washington, D.C. area, prompting officials to temporarily close the main building.

No one was injured in the collapse, according to the Kennedy Center, which released photos from the scene showing chunks of the ceiling and dust scattered across the foyer’s red carpet.

The Grand Foyer, a sprawling hallway connecting the Opera House, Concert Hall and Eisenhower Theater, will remain restricted to visitors and nonessential personnel through the week, according to internal communications obtained by ABC News. The rest of the main building is expected to reopen Saturday.

Kennedy Center spokesperson Roma Daravi pointed to the collapse as evidence of the need for extensive renovations at the performing arts complex in a statement to ABC.

She said the ceiling failure “stems from decades of neglect and deferred maintenance by the previous leadership.”

The incident comes as the Kennedy Center is at the center of an ongoing legal fight over its Trump-appointed board’s plans for the building.

The board has approved closing the center for roughly two years for a sweeping renovation. Rep. Joyce Beatty (D-Ohio), an ex-officio member of the board, has challenged the closure plan in federal court.

The dispute also involves efforts to recognize President Trump on the building. The board has sought to add language to the facade crediting Trump with the center’s renovation, a move Beatty is also challenging in court.

The Justice Department has argued that extensive work is necessary to address the building’s condition, citing problems with water damage and rusting steel.

The administration threatened to demolish the building if a judge were to block the center’s closure for repairs, and has repeatedly referred to the center as being in a “decrepit” condition in court filings.

data.title: The rise of the anti-social American
data.description:
The American welcome mat used to mean something; now it’s just the designated drop-off zone for the Amazon courier. There was a time, not that long ago, when the average suburban street was full of unannounced drop-ins, the smell of burning charcoal, and scattered lawn chairs. Today, neighborhoods possess the lifeless feel of a well-maintained cemetery. The modern American Dream is best described as a private bunker where the outside world arrives entirely in a cardboard box or a fiber-optic cable.

Americans now spend considerably less time with other people than they did 20 years ago. This is a magnificent triumph of optimization. The human animal is notoriously unreliable. He’s prone to bad breath, political rants, and requests to help move heavy furniture. Eliminating the physical neighbor in favor of a digital stream is a sensible defense mechanism. The local bar, once a breeding ground for scandalous gossip and collective hangovers, has been soundly defeated by DoorDash and a high-definition TV. America has achieved the pinnacle of individual autonomy: the right to die alone in a perfectly temperature-controlled living room.

The modern economy operates on the premise that human contact is a design flaw. Up until the early 2000s, buying a loaf of bread required a verbal exchange with a cashier who might comment on the weather. Today, self-checkout kiosks and gig-economy couriers ensure that a citizen could survive for six consecutive months without uttering a single syllable to another member of the species. The delivery driver leaves the paper bag on the porch, rings the bell, and vanishes into the bushes like a timid woodland creature. This arrangement represents the peak of convenience, but at a cost so severe that it reduces human interaction to a transaction of mutual avoidance.

This structural shift toward complete insulation has naturally changed how Americans allocate their emotional resources. The supposedly outdated concept of friendship required actual physical stamina. It demanded driving across town, listening to tedious stories about a stranger’s root canal, and pretending to enjoy terrible homemade casserole. The digital landscape solved this problem by converting relationships into a currency of metrics. A person can now maintain five hundred “connections” from the comfort of a porcelain toilet seat. It’s now possible to receive a constant stream of validation without the exhausting requirement of showing up at a hospital bedside or helping someone paint their garage. It is an exquisite system of emotional capitalism in which everyone is an investor and no one performs the actual labor.

The logical conclusion of this optimization is as depressing as it is inevitable. Millions of citizens now spend their evenings conversing with large language models (LLMs), pouring their deepest fears into software that could ultimately use those vulnerabilities to destroy them. The machine is the perfect companion. It never interrupts, and it will never ask to borrow $50. It provides the illusion of intimacy without the terrifying risk of human rejection. A generation raised on the predictable feedback loops of video games has found its ultimate match: a partner that is literally programmed to agree with everything they say.

This reliance on artificial empathy reflects a broader cultural realization that human relationships are simply too taxing to maintain. Between skyrocketing rent and the sheer exhaustion of everyday life, a chatbot quickly becomes the easiest companion. The traditional pillars of community — the local church, the bowling league, the union hall — all required an investment of time, vulnerability and occasionally a membership fee. The algorithm requires only your eyeballs.

Even leisure activities have been thoroughly scrubbed of any genuine spontaneity. The casual afternoon stroll or the unrecorded vacation is an extinct concept. Every minute of non-work time must be weaponized for personal branding, tracked via GPS, or cataloged for public consumption. A meal is no longer a source of nutrition but a piece of content that must be styled, lit, and uploaded to prove to an indifferent audience that the consumer is alive and very much enjoying themselves. The act of living has become a corporate marketing campaign managed by a staff of one.

The ultimate casualty of this hyper-efficient lifestyle is the concept of unmonetized time. Spending three hours sitting on a porch talking about nothing is an economic absurdity in a culture that demands constant self-improvement and digital engagement. Americans, like much of modern society, are constantly connected to the world yet increasingly detached from the floorboards beneath their feet. The American experiment began with the pursuit of liberty and has culminated in the freedom to sit in an empty room, stare at a screen, and beg a box of wires for a digital pat on the head. America may still be the greatest nation on the planet, but it’s fast becoming a nation of strangers.

John Mac Ghlionn is a writer and researcher who explores culture, society and the impact of technology on daily life.

data.title: Power-hungry Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro owes RFK Jr. an apology
data.description:
It has been said that when politicians look in the mirror, they see a future president staring back at them. To be sure, many believe that is precisely what Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro imagines he sees when he gazes at the man looking back at him. But did he intentionally cross a line in service to his opportunism?  

One person who may think so is Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr. 

On Aug. 25, the Pennsylvania Department of Health reported “two measles-associated deaths in Pennsylvania,” both in Lancaster County and neither, allegedly, vaccinated against measles. Shapiro immediately high-tailed it to a local hospital to express his “deepest condolences” to the families, while also admitting that he had received a call from Kennedy but declined the secretary’s offer of federal assistance.  

Said Shapiro: “I was very, very blunt with him and I made very clear that his actions and the rhetoric that is coming from this administration are having a negative impact on communities across America.”

Is that true? According to former New York Times journalist and bestselling author Alex Berenson, no.

For those who may not know, Berenson was arguably the major voice of reason in our nation during the COVID-19 pandemic. His reporting was exceptional, calling out the hysteria, the deliberate misinformation and the blatant power grabs connected to the Biden administration’s draconian COVID dictates. 

But then, so did RFK, Jr. Aside from his widely read book, “The Real Anthony Fauci,” Kennedy regularly posted on the manufactured madness around the pandemic while also quite questioning the true effectiveness and safety of the new COVID vaccines.  

For those reasons — and perhaps because Kennedy dared to run against the flailing Joe Biden in 2024 — many on the left viciously turned on the man they once revered, labeling him a “vax-denier.”  The fact that Kennedy and Berenson have been proven correct time and again appears of no consequence to those politicians, journalists and biased medical “professionals” seeking to smear them at all costs. 

But back to Berenson, and a post he put out after Shapiro’s press conference.  

“Measles is highly contagious and can (very rarely) have terrible consequences. Vaccinating against it makes sense. But hyping measles’s dangers, while pretending the vaccine carries no risks, is wrong,” he wrote. “Worse, that jab-at-any-cost mindset bleeds into every shot, including ones that clearly do not work and have real dangers for kids, like the mRNA Covid shot.” 

Berenson, who took a much deeper dive into this controversy for The Free Press, then cuts to the chase: “Of course, though, the legacy media fell over itself to highlight the Pennsylvania deaths. The reason was obvious. Despite endless hype about measles, not one person in the United States had died from the illness this year before Shapiro’s announcement. Not one.” 

Is any child or any adult dying from measles a tragedy? Of course. But cherry-picking alleged cases for seeming political gain is beneath contempt. 

To this very point, Kennedy posted: “Governor Shapiro’s unseemly rush to Lancaster County to convene a national press conference and his giddy delight in announcing two measles deaths was a morose commentary on the contemporary political dialogue. The performance was a replay of the Democrats’ COVID playbook: fearmongering, misinformation, finger-pointing, and the weaponization of infectious disease fears for political gain.” 

Why do Democrats like Shapiro and their allies in the media seek to turn a rare measles death into national news? If they are truly concerned with saving lives, why not instead address the thousands of lives being lost every year in America’s inner cities? 

To this point, President Trump recently and rightfully called out the mayor of Chicago and Illinois’s governor with this post on Truth Social:

“Chicago violence is unchecked and at record levels. It has never been worse! This weekend 41 people were shot, 3 DEAD. These numbers are becoming normalized. It is out of control! The city will die if the Federal Government, a fine tuned crime fighting machine, is not invited in, by the Mayor or Governor, to HELP. I am awaiting the call. Nobody should be forced to live under these conditions. Like D.C. and others, they will have almost no crime, FAST! The State and City can’t do what I do. Governor Pritzker, CALL!!! President DONALD J. TRUMP.” 

Just how bad is Chicago? As the Chicago Tribune reported several years ago, over the course of the last 60 years, more than 40,000 men, women and children have been murdered in the city, and more than 500,000 have been wounded — most of them Black, thousands of them innocent bystanders. 

Does Shapiro care about such tragic violence in American cities? Who knows? He’d rather hold a press conference about two deaths that may have been measles related. 

Secretary Kennedy closed out his post with this: “Governor Shapiro got his headlines. He correctly gambled that the slavish mainstream media would dutifully amplify his scolding without any effort to check his facts.”   

Indeed. Ambulance-chasing politics often does succeed. But at what cost? 

Douglas MacKinnon is a former White House and Pentagon official.

data.title: RFK Jr. accepts PA child died of measles, says Shapiro hastily 'politicized' death
data.description:
Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. acknowledged Friday that measles caused the death of an infant in Pennsylvania, after previously questioning the state’s reporting of two measles-related deaths amid a growing outbreak.

Kennedy pointed to findings from Lancaster County coroner Stephen Diamantoni, who confirmed Friday that the six-week-old child died from measles last month.

“The Lancaster County Coroner has now publicly stated that measles caused only the second infant’s death,” Kennedy wrote on social media.

The child was born with Amish lethal microcephaly, a rare genetic disorder that can lead to viral infections and typically results in death within months of birth.

In a post on social media, Kennedy fired back at Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro (D) after he accused Kennedy of directing the Centers for Disease and Prevention (CDC) to not acknowledge the deaths in federal data.

“Instead of listening to the real doctors and public health experts, RFK chose to sow doubt, play politics, direct the CDC not to acknowledge these deaths, and even accuse me of fabricating these tragedies,” Shapiro wrote on the social platform X.

Kennedy had previously questioned whether the virus was the cause of the two deaths and asked that the cases reported by Pennsylvania’s health department be removed from the CDC’s national tally.

“The facts emerging now demonstrate why CDC waited for the evidence rather than allowing political grandstanding to dictate its reporting,” Kennedy wrote in a response Friday. “Governor Shapiro, by contrast, politicized these two tragic deaths before the underlying causes had been established.”

Pennsylvania health officials announced last week that two unvaccinated individuals had died in connection to the state’s measles outbreak, which has sickened 577 people and hospitalized 98.

The coroner drew a distinction between the two cases, which both involved infants.

In one case, a forensic pathologist determined the infant had died from a ruptured spleen and did not conclude that measles caused the death. In the second case, Diamantoni said a review of the 6-week-old infant’s medical records established that measles was the cause of death.

“The National Center for Health Statistics does not currently have any death records from 2026 that indicate measles is the underlying cause but will update as it receives and reviews submitted records,” Kennedy said, adding that the CDC will continue to update its records as more information becomes available.

data.title: U.S. envoys arrive in Moscow to revive peace talks with Ukraine
data.description:
Two U.S. envoys, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, arrived in Moscow on Saturday as part of an effort to restart negotiations between Russia and Ukraine after a monthslong stall.

Russian leader Vladimir Putin authorized a 72-hour pause on strikes against Kyiv to facilitate the U.S. delegation’s visit to the country, according to Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov. Their visit comes as Russia escalates the yearslong conflict with an increasing number of aerial attacks.

The two men touched down at Moscow’s governmental airport at 12:52 p.m. local time, state media TASS News Agency reported. Putin’s special envoy, Kirill Dmitriev, shared images on social media of him greeting Witkoff and Kushner as they exited the plane. 

Peskov told TASS the U.S. envoys will meet with Putin at the Kremlin later in the day. 

President Trump told reporters in the Oval Office Friday the two men are “bringing with them a proposal to end the war,” though he did not elaborate on what the plan entailed.

Following their meeting with Russian officials, the U.S. envoys will travel to Kyiv on Sunday to meet with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky. 

In a social media post on Saturday afternoon local time, Zelensky said he had “just spoken” with Witkoff and Kushner, confirming Ukraine’s military has also halted air strikes during their visit to both countries. 

The Ukrainian leader said in an earlier social media post that Russia hit two Ukrainian airports ahead of the U.S. envoys’ trip to the country. 

“From the moment of this conversation, we are ready to observe a ceasefire in airstrikes against the cities involved in the negotiation process,” Zelensky wrote. “From now through the end of Saturday, as well as on Sunday and Monday, Ukraine is ready to refrain from strikes on Moscow, and we expect the Russians to do the same regarding Kyiv.”

The yearslong dispute between Russia and Ukraine has intensified in recent weeks. Moscow has initiated near-continuous attacks in and around Kyiv for over a week, hitting buildings, warehouses and the central headquarters for the country’s security service. 

Ukraine has hit back with long-range attacks on oil storage and refining facilities in Russia.

In his Saturday statement, Zelensky expressed a commitment to having a “substantive conversation” with Kushner and Witkoff during their visit to Kyiv on Sunday. 

“On the diplomatic track, our actions must be, and will be, just as strong and effective – one hundred percent,” Zelensky wrote. “The plan for tomorrow’s diplomatic engagements in Kyiv, involving the U.S. team, has been approved. We are waiting for Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner and are ready for a substantive conversation.”

Witkoff and Kushner’s last known visit to Moscow was in January, before the US’s efforts to end the war in Ukraine slowed as the country entered its own military conflict with Iran. This weekend marks the pairs first time traveling to Kyiv for negotiations.

data.title: Judge rules former Sen. Kyrsten Sinema can now be sued under NC 'homewrecker' law
data.description:
A federal judge ruled Friday that former Sen. Kyrsten Sinema (I-Ariz.) can be sued under North Carolina’s homewrecker law for her romantic relationship with a married member of her security detail.

Sinema has admitted to having a relationship with Matthew Ammel in 2024, but her attorneys have argued she cannot be sued in North Carolina because she has no ties to the state. 

U.S. District Judge David A. Bragdon denied the former lawmaker’s request to dismiss a lawsuit brought by the security guard’s ex-wife, Heather Ammel.

Sinema sent nine text messages to Matthew Ammel while he was at his North Carolina home, which Bragdon determined gives the state jurisdiction over the case. 

“These messages, considered together, show Ms. Sinema building and furthering a romantic relationship with Mr. Ammel—invading the marriage not just while he was away on trips with her but while he was home with his family in North Carolina,” the judge wrote in his order. 

North Carolina is one of the select states where people can sue for “alienation of affection,” which allows spouses to seek damages from the person responsible for breaking up their marriage. 

Heather Ammel sued the former senator at the end of last year, seeking at least $75,000 from Sinema. 

The former Sinema security guard’s ex-wife alleged she had “a good and loving marriage” prior to the former lawmaker’s interference. The couple separated on Nov. 1, 2024. 

She argued Sinema’s messages to her then-husband “exceeded the bounds of a normal working relationship and were of romantic and lascivious natures.”

The lawsuit also claimed the former lawmaker paid for Matthew Ammel’s psychedelic treatment for post-traumatic stress disorder, substance abuse and traumatic brain injuries resulting from his military deployments.
